title: What chemogenetics actually is
objective: Explain what a DREADD is and why a 'designer receptor + designer drug' lets you control one cell type remotely.

steps.title: The goal: a remote control for one cell type
steps.body: You've genetically defined a set of neurons ([[Cre]]/[[Flp]] — see C2/C3). Now you want to **turn them up or down in a living animal** and watch what changes. Chemogenetics does this with a drug: put an engineered receptor only in your cells, give a systemic compound, and only those cells respond.

steps.title: DREADD = Designer Receptor Exclusively Activated by a Designer Drug
steps.body: A [[DREADD]] is a **[[GPCR|G-protein-coupled receptor]] (GPCR) engineered so it ignores its natural ligand and instead responds only to an otherwise-inert drug**. The classic ones are mutated human muscarinic receptors. Because the drug is (meant to be) biologically inert on its own, cells *without* the DREADD shouldn't care that it's there.

steps.prompt: What makes a DREADD 'exclusive' to your cells of interest?
options: The drug is injected directly into those cells
Only cells engineered to express the DREADD can respond to the otherwise-inert drug
The drug only exists inside neurons
The receptor is destroyed in all other cells
steps.explanation: Specificity comes from expression, not from where the drug goes. The drug is given systemically and reaches everything; only DREADD-expressing cells transduce it into a signal.

steps.prompt: Why is it useful that a DREADD is a GPCR rather than an ion channel?
options: GPCRs act through the cell's own second-messenger machinery, nudging excitability over minutes
Ion channels can't be expressed in neurons
steps.explanation: DREADDs recruit endogenous G-protein pathways, giving slower, sustained, more physiological modulation over minutes-to-hours — the opposite end of the timescale from optogenetics' millisecond control. That trade-off (next lessons) is the whole reason to pick one tool over the other.

steps.setup: You give the DREADD drug to a mouse that was NEVER given the virus/allele to express the DREADD.
steps.prompt: What should happen to your target neurons, if the tool is behaving ideally?
options: Nothing — no DREADD means no designer response
steps.reveal: Ideally, nothing — that's the entire premise of an 'inert' drug. This is also why a DREADD-free animal given the drug is a required control (lesson C5-L4): it tests whether the drug does anything on its own.
